lead: Radio, inertial and satellite navigation is how a modern aircraft works out where it is, follows a guidance path down to the runway, and warns the crew before the aircraft reaches the ground. After this unit you can build a position fix from ranges, bearings or time differences, read an ILS deviation, size the drift of an inertial system, work one Kalman update by hand, and explain how radar, ADS-B and TAWS keep the aircraft separated and clear of terrain.
about: The unit follows one thread: measure something, turn it into a line of position, then combine lines until the answer is tight. 5.1 sets that geometry. 5.2 turns it into radio aids and 5.3 applies the same idea to landing. 5.4 and 5.5 move to sensors that need no ground station — gyroscopes, accelerometers and the inertial navigation system. 5.6 brings in GPS, 5.7 lists the errors that limit it, and 5.8 fuses GPS with the INS so each covers the other's weakness. 5.9 widens the picture to radar and shared surveillance data, and 5.10 closes with the warnings that keep the aircraft off the terrain.

chapters.idea: Every navigation system answers two questions — where am I, and which way am I going — by crossing measured lines of position drawn on a reference frame.
chapters.depth: Earth as a sphere and as an ellipsoid (WGS-84); latitude and longitude; great circle and rhumb line; nautical mile = 1852 m and knot = 1 nm/h; heading, track, bearing, radial and drift as four separate words. Position lines: circle (range), straight line (bearing), hyperbola (range difference), and the rho-theta, rho-rho and theta-theta fixing methods. Fix from two or three lines of position, the cocked hat, and why a cut angle near 90° gives the tightest fix. Reference frames ECEF, local NED and inertial. Accuracy against repeatability. Some syllabi call this 'navigation fundamentals' or 'position fixing'.

figure.title: From one measurement to a fix
figure.aria: A flow from a reference frame through one measurement to a single line of position, then two or more lines crossing to give a fix with its error ellipse.

chapters.example:
Two DME stations A and B are 130 nm apart on the ground. The aircraft's corrected DME reads 50 nm to A and 120 nm to B. Find the cut angle where the two position circles cross, and say whether this is a good fix.
Cosine rule at the aircraft: cos θ = (50² + 120² − 130²) ÷ (2 × 50 × 120) = (2500 + 14400 − 16900) ÷ 12000 = 0, so θ = 90°. A right-angle cut is the best possible geometry, so the fix is strong in both directions.
chapters.trap: Bearing and heading are not the same thing. A VOR radial of 030° means the aircraft sits on the 030° line going out from the station; the aircraft may be heading anywhere. Students also treat a great circle as a rhumb line and get the track wrong.
chapters.prereq: Basic trigonometry, and the altimeter and airspeed indicator from Unit 3 for the third dimension.
chapters.leave: Radio propagation and station errors to 5.2; Earth rate and the apparent drift it causes inside a gyro to 5.4 and 5.5.

chapters.idea: A radio aid either measures range or bearing to one known station (point source) or measures the difference in distance to two stations (hyperbolic), and each measurement draws one line of position.
chapters.depth: Point-source systems: ADF/NDB relative bearing, VOR (108–117.95 MHz, radial measured from the station, CVOR and DVOR), DME (UHF 962–1213 MHz, pulse pairs, slant range), TACAN, and VOR/DME pairing for a rho-theta fix. Hyperbolic systems: time difference of arrival gives a constant range difference, whose locus is a hyperbola with the two stations as foci; two differences (three stations) are needed for a fix. LORAN-C at 100 kHz on ground-wave chains, Decca, the withdrawn Omega, and the same principle reused by satellite navigation in 5.6. Formulas: DME ground range d = √(r² − h²); Δr = c·Δt; semi-major axis a = Δr/2; b² = c² − a², with c the half baseline. Accuracy against cut angle.

figure.aria: A classification tree splitting radio navigation aids into point-source systems that use one station and hyperbolic systems that compare the distance to two or more stations.

chapters.example:
A LORAN-C receiver measures a time difference of 100 µs between the master station and one secondary. The master–secondary baseline is 600 km. (a) Find the range difference Δr. (b) Find the semi-major and semi-minor axes of the hyperbola. (c) Which branch is the aircraft on?
(a) Δr = c·Δt = 3 × 10⁸ m/s × 100 × 10⁻⁶ s = 30 km.
(b) a = Δr/2 = 15 km. Half baseline c = 300 km, so b = √(300² − 15²) = √(90000 − 225) = 299.6 km.
(c) The secondary's signal arrives later, so the aircraft is farther from the secondary, that is, on the branch nearer the master.
chapters.trap: Two stations give one hyperbola, which is one line of position — not a fix. A hyperbolic fix needs three stations. Second trap: DME shows slant range; the ground distance is smaller, and at high altitude the difference is large.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for lines of position, cut angle and the nautical mile.
chapters.leave: ILS localizer and glideslope to 5.3; ranging codes and orbits to 5.6; radar, which also measures range, to 5.9.

chapters.idea: ILS and MLS guide an aircraft down a fixed approach path by broadcasting two beams that each define one angle in space — the localizer for left and right, the glideslope for up and down.
chapters.depth: ILS parts and their functions: localizer (108–112 MHz VHF, 40 channels, odd tenths of a MHz), glideslope (329.15–335 MHz UHF, paired channels, 150 kHz spacing), marker beacons at 75 MHz or a DME, and approach lighting. Amplitude modulation at 90 Hz and 150 Hz, and the difference in depth of modulation (DDM) as the guidance number. Standard values: localizer full-scale deflection 2.5° each side of centreline, glideslope full scale 0.7° (that is, ±0.35°), typical path angle 3°. Localizer: 90 Hz left, 150 Hz right. Glideslope: 150 Hz above the path, 90 Hz below. Categories CAT I (decision height 60 m / 200 ft, RVR 550 m), CAT II (30 m / 100 ft, RVR 300 m), CAT IIIA (below 30 m or no decision height, RVR 200 m), IIIB (RVR 50 m), IIIC (no limits). Advantages and limits: simple airborne receiver, but site-sensitive, straight approaches only, few channels. MLS: 5031–5091 MHz (about 5 GHz), time-referenced scanning beam, 200 channels, azimuth coverage about ±60°, elevation 0–20°, curved and segmented approaches, far less sensitive to siting, paired with DME-P for range. One line on GBAS and SBAS as the modern replacement.

figure.title: Two beams, two deviations
figure.aria: Two parallel receiver chains, one for the localizer and one for the glideslope, each turning a modulation difference into a needle deflection on the same display.

chapters.example:
An aircraft is on a 3° ILS glide path and the DME reads 5.0 nm to the threshold. (a) What height should the aircraft be at? (b) The glideslope receiver measures a DDM of 0.05 with 150 Hz stronger. How far off path is the aircraft, and on which side?
(a) 5 nm = 5 × 6076 = 30,380 ft. Height = 30,380 × tan 3° = 30,380 × 0.05241 = 1592 ft (about 1590 ft, or roughly 318 ft per nm).
(b) Full-scale DDM is 0.155 at 0.35°. Deflection = 0.05 ÷ 0.155 = 0.32 of full scale, so 0.32 × 0.35° = 0.11°. 150 Hz stronger means the aircraft is above the path.
chapters.trap: The two axes do not share a rule: on the localizer 90 Hz is left and 150 Hz is right, but on the glideslope 150 Hz is above the path and 90 Hz is below. Students mix the two, and also confuse the localizer band with the glideslope band.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for lines of position and 5.2 for the point-source idea and DME ranging.
chapters.leave: PFD and EADI symbology to Unit 4; autopilot coupling and autoland to Unit 1; SBAS and GBAS to 5.6.

chapters.idea: A spinning mass keeps its axis fixed in inertial space, and when a torque is applied the axis moves at right angles to that torque — that is precession, and every gyroscopic instrument is built on it.
chapters.depth: Angular momentum H = Iω, with I the moment of inertia in kg·m² and ω the spin rate in rad/s, so H is in kg·m²/s. Rigidity in space, two degrees of freedom against three, gimbals and gimbal lock, caging and erection. Torque and precession: T = dH/dt and steady precession rate Ω = T/H = T/(Iω). Direction of precession: dH points along T, so the spin axis moves at 90° to the push, in the sense of the spin. Nutation: the short wobble that follows a suddenly applied torque, and how damping removes it. Drift: real drift from bearing friction and imbalance, and apparent drift from Earth rate (15.04°/h at the poles, zero at the equator) and transport rate over the curved Earth. Instruments: attitude indicator (vertical gyro, erected to the local vertical), heading indicator (directional gyro, set to magnetic north, drifts and must be reset), turn coordinator (rate gyro, shows rate of turn and roll). Ring laser and fibre-optic gyros are named here and used in 5.5. Some syllabi call nutation 'the wobble' and precession 'the topple'.

figure.title: Torque, momentum and precession
figure.aria: A cycle in which a spinning rotor gains angular momentum, an applied torque tilts that momentum vector, and the steady precession follows at right angles, with nutation as the short-lived side branch.

chapters.example:
A gyro rotor has moment of inertia I = 0.02 kg·m² and spins at 24,000 rpm. A steady torque of 0.01 N·m is applied. Find H and the precession rate in degrees per minute.
ω = 24,000 × 2π ÷ 60 = 2513 rad/s.
H = Iω = 0.02 × 2513 = 50.3 kg·m²/s.
Ω = T/H = 0.01 ÷ 50.3 = 1.99 × 10⁻⁴ rad/s = 0.0114 °/s = 0.68 °/min.
Context: Earth rate is 15 °/h, that is 0.25 °/min, so even a tiny stray torque is comparable to the signal the gyro is meant to measure.
chapters.trap: Students draw the precession in the direction of the push. The axis actually moves at right angles to the torque, in the direction that carries H toward T. The second trap is quoting nutation as if it were the steady motion; it is the transient that damping kills.
chapters.prereq: Basic rotational mechanics — torque, moment of inertia, angular velocity — and Unit 1 for the autopilot that consumes these signals.
chapters.leave: Accelerometers and the full inertial mechanization to 5.5, including the internal detail of ring laser and fibre-optic gyros.

chapters.idea: An inertial navigation system measures its own acceleration and rotation and integrates them to get velocity and position without any outside help — accurate for minutes and drifting for hours.
chapters.depth: Accelerometers: proof mass, force rebalance, output specific force f, which is proper acceleration, not acceleration in space; gravity is not felt and must be added back. Units of g (1 g = 9.81 m/s²), bias and scale factor. Gyros as rate sensors: ring laser, fibre optic, dynamically tuned and MEMS, with bias quoted in °/h. Frames: inertial, ECEF, NED and body, and the direction cosine matrix or quaternion that carries one into another. Two mechanizations: gimballed stable platform against strapdown, where sensors are bolted to the airframe and the mathematics does the stabilising. The block diagram of essential components: IMU → attitude → resolve f into the navigation frame → add gravity → integrate once for velocity → integrate again for position. Schuler tuning: the loop is tuned to T = 2π√(R/g) = 84.4 min so the platform stays level as the aircraft crosses the curved Earth. Alignment by levelling and gyrocompassing. Error growth: accelerometer bias b gives position error ½bt²; gyro bias ε gives tilt εt, horizontal acceleration error gεt and position error about gεt³/6.

figure.title: Strapdown inertial mechanization
figure.aria: The inertial chain from the sensor block through attitude and frame conversion, adding gravity, integrating twice to position, with a dashed Schuler feedback holding the platform level.

chapters.example:
An inertial system is aligned and then runs without aiding for 100 s with an accelerometer bias of 1 mg along the horizontal. (a) Find the velocity and position error at 100 s. (b) Separately, a gyro bias of 0.01 °/h tilts the platform for one hour — find the position error.
(a) b = 1 mg = 0.00981 m/s². Velocity error = bt = 0.00981 × 100 = 0.98 m/s. Position error = ½bt² = 0.5 × 0.00981 × 100² = 49 m.
(b) Tilt = 0.01° = 1.745 × 10⁻⁴ rad. Horizontal acceleration error = g × tilt = 9.81 × 1.745 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.71 × 10⁻³ m/s². Over t = 3600 s: velocity error = 1.71 × 10⁻³ × 3600 = 6.2 m/s; position error = ½ × 1.71 × 10⁻³ × 3600² = 11.1 km.
chapters.trap: An accelerometer does not measure acceleration in space; it measures specific force, so gravity must be added back. The second trap is assuming position error grows linearly — it grows as t² from accelerometer bias and roughly as t³ from gyro bias.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 for gyro behaviour, 5.1 for the frames, and the accelerometer transducer material in Unit 4.
chapters.leave: The filter that arrests this drift to 5.8; satellite position fixes to 5.6; the flight management system's use of the answer to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A satellite navigation receiver finds its position by timing the arrival of coded radio signals from four or more satellites whose positions are known from their broadcast orbits.
chapters.depth: GPS (NAVSTAR) constellation: 24 slots as the baseline, 6 orbital planes, 55° inclination, about 20,200 km altitude, period 11 h 58 min. Signals: L1 1575.42 MHz, L2 1227.60 MHz, L5 1176.45 MHz; C/A code at 1.023 Mchip/s and P(Y) at 10.23 Mchip/s; PRN codes and code-phase ranging. Navigation message: ephemeris, almanac, clock corrections, ionospheric coefficients. Ranging: pseudorange ρ = c(t_receive − t_transmit); four unknowns x, y, z and receiver clock offset δt need four satellites, and the solution is a small matrix solve whose quality is set by DOP. Orbital mechanics: Kepler elements, why a 12 h orbit gives a repeating ground track, and why clock stability (rubidium, caesium) matters. Segments: space, control, user. Other constellations: GLONASS (FDMA, 64.8° inclination), Galileo, BeiDou, NavIC (regional, geostationary plus inclined geosynchronous satellites). Augmentation: SBAS such as GAGAN, WAAS and EGNOS, GBAS, and receiver-side ABAS.

figure.title: From broadcast code to position
figure.aria: The receiver chain from a satellite broadcasting a coded signal with its own clock and orbit, through correlation and pseudorange, to a four-unknown solution giving position and receiver clock bias.

chapters.example:
A GPS satellite is at a slant range of 20,200 km. (a) How long does its signal take to arrive? (b) The receiver clock is fast by 3 µs — what range error does that add to every pseudorange? (c) Why does the receiver need four satellites rather than three?
(a) t = 20,200 km ÷ 299,792.458 km/s = 0.0674 s = 67.4 ms.
(b) Δρ = c·Δt = 2.998 × 10⁸ × 3 × 10⁻⁶ = 899 m, about 0.9 km.
(c) The unknowns are x, y, z and the receiver clock offset δt — four unknowns need four equations, so four satellites.
chapters.trap: Pseudorange is not the geometric range; it carries the receiver clock error and propagation delay. And three satellites give three equations for four unknowns, so the receiver clock bias alone forces a fourth satellite.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for frames and trilateration, and 5.2 for the point-source idea and time-based ranging.
chapters.leave: The size and cure of each error to 5.7; combining the fix with an INS to 5.8; ADS-B position source and TAWS position source to 5.9 and 5.10.

chapters.idea: GPS accuracy is set by four groups of error — satellite clocks and orbits, the ionosphere, the troposphere, and local effects at the antenna — and each responds to a different cure.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this unit at this depth; keep it to the error budget and the two atmospheres. Satellite clock offset and drift, corrected by the broadcast polynomial, plus relativistic and Sagnac effects; ephemeris error. Ionosphere: free electrons, total electron content, group delay that grows as 1/f², typically 5–15 m at zenith on L1 and much worse near the horizon and at solar maximum; the Klobuchar model in the broadcast message, dual-frequency L1/L5 removal, and scintillation. Troposphere: non-dispersive, about 2.5 m at zenith (roughly 2.3 m dry plus 0.2 m wet), growing as 1/sin(elevation) to tens of metres low on the horizon, cured by models only. Multipath and receiver noise. Dilution of precision: position error = UERE × DOP, with HDOP and VDOP named. One line each on RAIM and on why differential GPS removes common errors.

figure.aria: Layers along the signal path from satellite to receiver, each labelled with the typical size of the error it adds.

chapters.example:
An ionospheric delay of 12.0 m is measured on L1 at 1575.42 MHz. (a) Predict the delay on L5 at 1176.45 MHz. (b) If the remaining user equivalent range error is 5 m and HDOP is 1.8, find the one-sigma horizontal position error.
(a) Delay scales as 1/f², so d₂ = d₁ × (f₁/f₂)² = 12.0 × (1575.42 ÷ 1176.45)² = 12.0 × 1.793 = 6.7 m. (Equivalently 12.0 × 0.5576.)
(b) σ = UERE × HDOP = 5 × 1.8 = 9 m.
chapters.trap: The 1/f² law applies to the ionosphere only. The troposphere is non-dispersive, so a dual-frequency receiver does not remove it. Also, the satellite clock is already corrected by the broadcast, not by the atmosphere models.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 for the signal structure and the pseudorange, and 5.1 for the idea of dilution of precision.
chapters.leave: The Kalman treatment of these errors, as process and measurement noise, to 5.8.

chapters.idea: A Kalman filter blends the smooth but drifting INS with the noisy but bounded GPS, weighting each one by how much it is trusted at that moment.
chapters.depth: Why a filter and not a fix: both sources are wrong in different ways, and both carry a stated uncertainty. State vector x, covariance P, and the two steps. Predict: x = Fx + Bu and P = FPFᵀ + Q. Update: innovation y = z − Hx, gain K = PHᵀ(HPHᵀ + R)⁻¹, x ← x + Ky, P ← (I − KH)P. Meaning of Q (process noise, how much the model is distrusted), R (measurement noise), P (current uncertainty, shrinking with each fix). Loosely coupled (GPS position and velocity), tightly coupled (raw pseudoranges, so a fix can survive with fewer than four satellites) and ultra-tight (receiver aided by the INS). Coasting through a GPS outage as P grows, and feeding the corrections back to reset the inertial sensors. Some syllabi call the whole subject 'multisensor navigation'.

figure.title: Predict–update loop
figure.aria: A loop where the inertial mechanization predicts state and covariance, a GPS fix enters with its own noise, the Kalman gain sets the weight, and the update corrects both the output and the sensors themselves.

chapters.example:
One-dimensional case. The INS gives a position of 1000 m with variance 100 m². A GPS fix at the same instant gives 1050 m with variance 25 m². Find the Kalman gain, the blended position and the new variance.
K = P ÷ (P + R) = 100 ÷ (100 + 25) = 0.8.
Blended position = 1000 + 0.8 × (1050 − 1000) = 1000 + 40 = 1040 m.
New variance = (1 − K) × P = 0.2 × 100 = 20 m², so σ = 4.5 m — better than either source alone.
chapters.trap: K is not a fixed percentage or a tuned constant; it is recomputed from P and R at every step. Second trap: the innovation is measurement minus prediction, z − Hx, so the sign matters when the two disagree.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 for the INS, 5.6 and 5.7 for the GPS fix and its error budget.
chapters.leave: The flight management system's use of the blended solution and guidance laws to Unit 6; the autopilot loops that fly it to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Radar finds range from the travel time of an echo and bearing from the antenna direction, and surveillance systems — including the broadcast ADS-B — share that picture between aircraft and the ground.
chapters.depth: Pulse radar blocks: transmitter, duplexer, antenna, receiver, threshold, display. Radar equation R_max = [P_t G² λ² σ ÷ ((4π)³ P_min)]^¼, with P_t transmitted power, G antenna gain, λ wavelength, σ radar cross-section, P_min minimum detectable power. Range resolution = cτ/2 for pulse width τ; unambiguous range = c/(2·PRF). Doppler shift f_d = 2v_r/λ for radial speed v_r. Primary surveillance radar uses the skin echo; secondary surveillance radar interrogates at 1030 MHz and receives replies at 1090 MHz, with Mode A identity, Mode C altitude and Mode S addressing. ADS-B: extended squitter at 1090 MHz, 112-bit messages, roughly two per second, position from the aircraft's own GNSS, plus velocity and identity; ADS-B Out against ADS-B In; TIS-B and FIS-B; TCAS/ACAS as a separate cooperative system on the same transponders. Shorter coverage of radar altimeter (FMCW, height above ground), weather radar (reflectivity and Doppler) and mapping or multimode radar, which only some syllabi list.

figure.title: Three sources, one track picture
figure.aria: Three surveillance sources feeding one tracker, which fuses their plots into tracks that appear on a controller screen or a cockpit display.

chapters.example:
A pulse radar has PRF = 1000 Hz and pulse width 1 µs. (a) Find the maximum unambiguous range. (b) Find the range resolution. (c) Find the Doppler shift for an aircraft closing at 300 kt when the radar works at 1030 MHz.
(a) R_max = c ÷ (2 × PRF) = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 2000 = 150 km.
(b) ΔR = cτ/2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 1 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 2 = 150 m.
(c) 300 kt = 154.3 m/s, λ = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.03 × 10⁹ = 0.291 m, f_d = 2 × 154.3 ÷ 0.291 = 1060 Hz, about 1.06 kHz.
chapters.trap: PRF sets the unambiguous range and pulse width sets the resolution; students swap the two. The factor 2 for the round trip goes missing in both formulas. And ADS-B is a broadcast, not an interrogation — nothing is sent to the aircraft to prompt it.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for range and bearing as lines of position, and Unit 4 for the displays that show the traffic picture.
chapters.leave: The radar altimeter's output is used in 5.10; the GNSS position source is 5.6; TCAS resolution advisories and the autopilot response to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: TAWS warns the crew before the aircraft flies into terrain, using a radio altimeter for the near-ground reactive modes and a terrain database plus position for the look-ahead modes.
chapters.depth: Why it exists: controlled flight into terrain, where a serviceable aircraft is flown into ground the crew did not see. GPWS modes 1 to 7: Mode 1 excessive descent rate, Mode 2 excessive terrain closure rate with separate flap-up and flap-down envelopes, Mode 3 altitude loss after take-off, Mode 4 unsafe terrain clearance with gear and flap cases, Mode 5 excessive glideslope deviation when below the path, Mode 6 advisory callouts such as minimums and too low gear, Mode 7 windshear. All the reactive modes use radio altitude, so they look down, not ahead. TAWS/EGPWS adds a terrain database, GNSS position and look-ahead computation, giving forward-looking terrain avoidance and an alert roughly half a minute or more before predicted impact; caution level in amber, warning level in red, with the classic aural calls sink rate, terrain, pull up, too low gear, glideslope. Inhibit switches, nuisance warnings near steep approaches, and the limits: database currency, position error, unlit obstacles.

figure.aria: A tree splitting terrain warnings into the reactive ground proximity modes that measure height below the aircraft and the look-ahead alerts that use a terrain database with the aircraft's position.

chapters.example:
An aircraft is at 1800 ft above ground level, descending at 1800 ft/min towards level terrain, with TAWS look-ahead set to alert 30 s before predicted impact. (a) Find the time to impact now. (b) When does the alert come and at what height? (c) The altimeter sub-scale is set 5 hPa wrong — how much barometric height error does that add?
(a) Time = 1800 ÷ 1800 = 1 min = 60 s.
(b) 60 s is more than 30 s, so no alert yet. The alert comes when time to impact reaches 30 s, that is after 30 s of further descent, at 900 ft AGL.
(c) Near the surface 1 hPa ≈ 27 ft, so 5 hPa ≈ 135 ft. The reactive modes use radio altitude and are unaffected; the look-ahead path uses this barometric height, so the error matters there.
chapters.trap: GPWS is reactive and looks down with the radio altimeter; TAWS look-ahead is predictive and needs a database plus a position. Students also confuse Mode 5 (glideslope deviation, only where an ILS is tuned) with Mode 1 (sink rate), and quote barometric altitude where the mode actually uses radio altitude.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 for the glideslope behind Mode 5, the radar altimeter in 5.9, the GNSS position in 5.6, and the altimeter in Unit 3.
chapters.leave: Warning display symbology and aural priority to Unit 4; stall warning and other protection systems to Unit 2.
